title: Gandhi, Kasturba, and Goat's Milk: A Legalistic Compromise
summary: When doctors and Kasturba pointed out that his vow specifically intended cow and buffalo milk, Gandhi joked that doctors and wives are far better at finding legal loopholes than barristers.
keywords: Gandhi, Kasturba, and Goat's Milk: A Legalistic Compromise
full_text:
Mahatma Gandhi pursued dietary experiments with uncompromising discipline.

In 1912, distressed by the cruel treatment of dairy cows and buffaloes, Gandhi had taken a strict vow: he would never consume animal milk for the rest of his life.

In 1918, during the arduous Kheda agrarian campaign, Gandhi was struck down by severe dysentery. His body wasted away to forty kilograms. Physicians warned that without the protein and fats found in milk, his heart would fail.

Gandhi remained adamantly unyielding: "I took a solemn vow before God. I would rather die than violate my truth!"

Standing beside his sickbed, his wife Kasturba Gandhi listened with a knowing smile. She intervened gently:
"Bapu! When you took that vow in South Africa, what was in your mind?"

"I was thinking of the cruel treatment inflicted upon cows and buffaloes," Gandhi replied.

Kasturba smiled triumphantly:
"Then your vow applied only to cow's milk and buffalo's milk! You never took a vow against **goat's milk**! A goat is neither a cow nor a buffalo!"

The attending physician exclaimed: "Magnificent! Mrs. Gandhi's legal interpretation is watertight! Goat's milk will save your life without breaching your conscience!"

Gandhi looked at Kasturba, a sheepish grin spreading across his face:
"Alas! It seems that my wife and my physicians are far more cunning at discovering legal loopholes than any barrister trained at the London Inns of Court!
While my conscience whispers that I am bending the spirit of my vow, my duty to serve India compels me to accept your clever verdict. Bring the goat's milk!"

He drank the milk, regained his vitality, and continued leading the freedom struggle for another thirty years—nourished solely by goat's milk.
moral: Principles must serve life, not destroy it; the loving counsel of family can illuminate paths where rigid dogma blinds us.

By disguising it as fruit juice
